newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Baht devaluation is no economic cure-all -analysts.
newsitem.headline: Baht devaluation is no economic cure-all -analysts.

text.p: In a market awash with talk of an imminent devaluation of the Thai baht, analysts took a step back on Friday to look at the impact and potential problems an officially sanctioned drop in its value may bring.
They certainly do not see it as a cure-all.

Speculators burned by the Bank of Thailand's restriction of baht outflows saw a bright new day dawning with the resignation on Thursday of finance minister Amnuay Viravan, although the Bank of Thailand again stressed there would be no devaluation.
Devaluation is not the paliative it may seem at first glance and analysts said it was doubtful it would even allow interest rates to come down in the near term.

With a current account deficit around six percent of Gross Domestic Product (GDP), any lessening of the central bank resolve would probably lead to a further capital outflow and rates would have to be kept high or raised to prevent a currency meltdown, they said.
It could also give a sharp prod to import price inflation.

But the main reason the Thai authorities do not want to give into a devalution is that they do not want to increase the debt burden of ailing firms, particularly in the financial sector, given the very high level of off-shore debt.

"A 10 to 20 percent drop in the value of the currency, which are the sort of numbers being bandied around in the market, would not go down at all well with firms and finance houses with unhedged overseas debts," said Kobus Van Der Wath, regional head of treasury economics at Standard Chartered in Singapore.
Thailand may not need to boost exports by devaluing immediately and making its goods cheaper overseas. Some analysts are already looking for a rise in export growth this year.

"The fundamentals haven't changed and corporates remain weak from the overseas liabilities burden so a devaluation now would cure nothing at all," said Chiang Yao Chye, economist at CIBC Wood Gundy in Singapore.
But that does not mean the baht should not eventually be allowed to find it own level. Analysts say that is essential if Thailand wants to attract sustained and long-term fund flows.

Last week's announcement that Thailand would adopt a Singapore style foreign exchange regime was seen as flawed as a long-term policy simply because Thailand has a current account deficit and Singapore a surplus.

"Overseas investment is needed to fund the deficit so deterring foreign investment by imposing a rock-hard exchange rate scheme so investors have no flexibility is not much of an option'" said one analyst at a European bank here.
So what is in store for the baht, assuming the Thai authorities and central bank do stand their ground for now?
Some analysts believe Thailand will eventually move towards a more flexible exchange rate policy. One way would be to widen the band in which the onshore baht is allowed to trade.
The Exchange Equalization Fund (EEF), under the Bank of Thailand, announces a daily fixing for US$/baht with a spread of four satangs at which it stands ready to buy or sell from resident banks.
Widening the band now would simply result in a de facto devalution given the current lack of confidence and poor background economic fundamentals.
But further down the road -- perhaps much further -- it would help inject more flexibility and let Thailand become a financal centre and promote the baht as a regional currency.

"I think they will ultimately move to make the baht more flexible and one way to do that would be to widen the band...I really don't think the Bank of Thailand or the government see outright devaluation as an option," CIBC's Chye said.
